history.content: Can I mix two insecticides so the spray works better?

What you can do to get rid of the insects better than mixing is to look at the pest closely: how many insects are on the plant, whether the damage has started in one spot or all over, and whether it follows the window or the edge of the field, and whether it appeared after rain or a dry spell. Then pick the insecticide that name covers, and use it at the rate the label says. history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga is controlled by sowing extra-early varieties that reach maturity in 55-75 days, placing the seeds 3-5 cm deep with 2-3 seeds per pocket. When the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, spray a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel, never using neem powder alone. One kilogram of this mixture is enough for about 1,500-2,000 plants, so calculate the required amount for your field. Repeat the spray every 8-10 days while the crop is still young. Next, pull every striga plant from the field and destroy them to eliminate the source of the flower power. Then, plan to plant a grain legume such as soybean, groundnut or cowpea in the same season, using the striga-tolerant variety you obtained from ICAT. history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides and they do not mix. Combining them increases the product's toxicity for the pest and for the person spraying it, and it also treats for a wrong pest. The correct approach is to identify the pest first, then get the right product at the right rate from ICAT. If you mistake one for the other, the wrong spray will kill the wrong pest and leave residues that fuel further growth. Keep the sprayer mask with you and wear it properly when you mix.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins, what should I do?

draws.answer: That is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you ever see angular water-soaked spots with wilting, that is bacterial blight, not cassava mosaic. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Mix the remaining leucaena with grasses and cereal residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Change the feed composition slowly over several days. Keep clean water always available and provide a mineral or salt source. If the gums or throat remain swollen, see the veterinary service.

history.content: I heard about brown streak in cassava, can you tell me how to keep it from ruining my harvest?

draws.answer: Brown streak disease is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. First, walk the field and pull out any cassava plants that display chlorotic spots, dark streaks along the veins and shoot die-back, and destroy them. After removal, remove and destroy any plants that show gum exudation on the stem and disinfect your tools between each plant. Then, for the next planting, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves, no streaks, no gum, and only healthy stems. Obtain clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to verify the diagnosis.

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: The yellowing of the lower leaves after a sudden drop in nitrogen shows that the plant cannot absorb enough nitrogen from the soil. First, read the leaves before buying anything; the uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger, not a disease. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because on depleted soil the mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back. Third, bring back organic matter by adding manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. Fourth, include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, see ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

After you have removed the Striga, ask ICAT for the approved seed for the sorghum variety you will plant. If you need confirmation of the weed problem, see ICAT.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to sorghum, and you must pull it out as soon as you see it. First, look for the purple or pink-flowered Striga plants that grow in dense mats on the field floor. When you pull a striga plant, cut it at ground level to remove the whole root system, because the nutrients from the root stay in the soil. Then, return the soil to its organic matter by spreading manure, adding compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Choose a legume such as cowpea or groundnut for the next season to reduce the need for this control. For advice on the best method for your plot, see ICAT.

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is the legume harvest issue. Nutrient deficiency shows yellowing of the lower leaves from the bottom up with no spike. To manage it, do not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years, rotate with a legume, and use a tolerant variety. It is not Striga, it is Cercospora leaf-spot fungi that appear as dark round spots, yellow leaves and shoot die-back. Striga is a parasitic plant that takes root in cereal fields, not a fungal disease. To tell them apart, look for the defined spots and dead-heart symptoms; a fungus gives those signs. Because it is a disease, you should remove or bury the Striga before sowing, not add fertilizer. For the next season, plant a cereal on that land and use a tolerant variety. See ICAT for diagnosis.

history.content: I see a pink-flowered weed clinging to the base of my sorghum and the plants look short. What should I do?

draws.answer: That weed is a common problem on sorghum and can reduce harvest yield. Plant a cereal on the same plot next season and ask ICAT for the recommended seed to use. Prior to sowing, ask ICAT to verify the variety's suitability for your area and season. Put two to three seeds in each pocket spaced one to one and five to three for extra-early or intermediate types, using six to eight weeks of the first weeding for the crop to be harvested. After the first weeding, carry out the third weeding as a short pause before the sorghum reaches panicle initiation. For the right variety, see ICAT.

The weed is the straw vinaigrette of the sorghum. When the sorghum is still young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with a bowl of water into each funnel; one kilogram treats roughly 1,500-2,000 plants. Repeat the treatment every 8-10 days while the sorghum is still young. Do not apply neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the plant, always use the mixed formula. At panicle initiation, split a kilogram of the prepared mixture into each plant. After you harvest, destroy or deep-bury the sorghum stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If you need a larger field application, see ICAT.

history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Do not grow your second crop on the same plot for longer than two years, which is the rule against sharing soil. For the right variety, go to ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink-flowered weed at the base, how can I manage it?

draws.answer: The pink-flowered Striga that grows on Striga plants in your sorghum field is the problem you are facing. Sow a legume such as cowpea or groundnut immediately after the sorghum and cut the Striga plants at ground level so they do not compete. When the sorghum is in its two-week period of tillering and heading, apply urea at a rate of 100 kg per hectare. Then make a pinch of groundnut, cotton or soya powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, repeating every eight to ten days while the plants are small, and pull the Striga from the soil surface. If you have a large block of sorghum, ask ICAT for the correct spacing for your area.

The pink-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that must be removed before the sorghum flowers. Sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3 to 5 grains per pocket at 3 to 5 cm depth and using 6 to 8 kg per hectare of treated seed. At 2 to 3 weeks thin the sorghum to 2 plants per pocket and perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After the sorghum is in, perform the second weeding without disturbing the ridges. Follow with the expected Striga flowering period and pull it before the sorghum blooms. If you need help matching a variety to a striga-tolerant sorghum, see ICAT.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, the two products do not mix. The approved products are Insecticide Residue Management (IRM) product 1, a panel of products listed on the label, and the steps are to read the label before any mixing, to weigh the product, to mix until the colour is even, to apply the amount, and to take off any leaves that were not coated. Adding another product changes nothing; the amount changes, and the product you are mixing may not be approved in the rest of your spraying.

No, and two of the reasons make it clear. First, a compound acts on more than one thing at once: it dissolves the insects with its solvent and removes the honey and other substances that would otherwise keep them from flying, and the act of spraying itself makes them move and squirm. A strong enough jet of water would wash off the insects that had simply settled underneath. Second, the product is not a mixture of what you already have, because the brochure says one compound is often the right choice only on its own properties, and two different compounds would not sit on a single formula. So the strength stays on the bottle, and the method stays on the application.

history.content: My sheep are dying fast from a disease that looks like PPR, what steps save the rest?

draws.answer: It is not Pappie, it is gall sickness. Because the two are not the same, a wrong drug will not work, and a guess can harm the animals and the livestock trade. Call the veterinary service today; they will tell you which disease it is and give the right medication and its dose. Tell the vet the urine colour, because red to black indicates redwater and yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on every animal in the herd. Never reuse a needle between animals. The veterinary service is the only one to see for this.

Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen receives enough roughage. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days. Provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the sheep continue to die or show drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, contact the veterinary service.

history.content: My sorghum is stunted and I notice a pink-flowered plant wrapping its stems near the ground. How can I manage this?

draws.answer: Pink-flowered stunting with a wrapped stem indicates a so-called "blooming issue" caused by a flower thinning problem, not a disease. Avoid using only groundnut or cowpea as a legume because they do not resolve this symptom. Sow a legume such as cowpea or groundnut early in the season and cut the legume stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules in the soil. Then rotate a cereal after the legume and cut the old legume stems at ground level. If you later see window-pane holes in the whorl leaves or a dead-heart symptom, go to ICAT for diagnosis.

The pink-flowered stunt plant around the base is a clear sign of groundnut leaf spot. Do not grow groundnut on that land year after year, rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear or bury old groundnut trash. Harvest on schedule to avoid pod loss from weakened plants. For variety selection or fungicide advice, see ICAT.

history.content: How much urea should I mix with manure to control Striga on my sorghum?

draws.answer: You should use about 100 kg of urea for a hectare of sorghum after you have cut the Striga with the plant before it flowers. First, sow sorghum on light, well-drained soil and perform the first weeding at the right time. Do not grow sorghum after maize because striga plants will invade. When the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, place the 100 kg of urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, making sure the fertilizer does not touch the plant to prevent burning. Pull the Striga plants before they flower and keep the sorghum into the fall for the legume. For any variety or rate questions, go to ICAT.

You should first open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Then, when the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. I cannot give you the exact amount of manure to mix, and you should ask a local extension officer for that detail.

history.content: My field has some cassava with twisted leaves and others with brown rot inside the roots. Which problem am I dealing with?

draws.answer: You are facing cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Next, for the new planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then plant an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. No spray will cure an infected plant, so remove the problematic material and avoid any spraying. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

The symptoms you see are cassava mosaic disease and cassava bacterial blight. Then, when you plant new cassava, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no distortion, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.

history.content: I found a pink flower weed hugging the bottom of my short sorghum stalks, what steps should I take?

Then rotate or intercrop the sorghum with a legume such as cowpea or soybean so the plant does not stay in the field for long. When the sorghum is trough 2-3 weeks after sowing, perform the first weeding to keep the field tidy. For a reliable soil-conditioned variety, see ICAT.

The pink-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that reduces the yield of your sorghum. First, stop planting your sorghum on the same plot in consecutive seasons to break the cycle of the parasite. Then, when the sorghum harvest is at about 50-60 days, perform the first weeding to keep the field weed-free. Next, pick up the Striga clinging to the base of the sorghum plants and destroy it to prevent it from flowering. After that, sow a legume such as cowpea or soybean to add nitrogen to the soil. For any pest issues, go to ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

draws.answer: The problem is groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora leaf-spot fungi. First, avoid planting groundnut on the same plot consecutively; instead rotate the field with a cereal crop. Second, use a tolerant groundnut variety when you plant again. Third, after harvest, clear or bury all the groundnut residues so the fungi cannot survive in the soil. Fourth, harvest your groundnut crop on schedule to prevent pod drop from weakened plants. For advice on the best tolerant variety or whether a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my flock?

draws.answer: The disease is called fowl pox. First, isolate every bird that still has dry form signs from the sick ones. Then give the isolated birds extra feed and clean water while the disease runs its course. Next, cut down mosquito breeding by removing standing water and keeping the area tidy. After that, vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox. Finally, if you see the wet form with mouth or throat lesions, go to the veterinary service.

The disease is called fowl pox. First isolate any animals showing raised wart-like scabs on the comb, wattles or face. Clean your cutting tools with a disinfectant before you work on the next plant. Plant a cassava variety that is resistant to cassava bacterial blight. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

Yes, cassava brown streak disease shows yellow or pale mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves, while bacterial blight presents as wilting, then shoot die-back, and has angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and sometimes gum on stems. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot. To get clean resistant cuttings, see ITRA.

history.content: Can I mix two insecticides in one spray to make it stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides and no stronger product does. A combination is not making the product stronger, it is putting a bigger load on the insect: the active ingredient in each product, its rate against the insect it has been tested on, the weather. What does not change when you add more is the time the insect is waiting before you spray, because that is the window the product was formulated for. For any product, read the label and ask ICAT where to buy the product itself.

No, and combining two insecticides does not make it stronger. The reason is that the molecules interact differently, and the rate at which a chemical reaches the pest is the same whether you mix. When you mix, you also mix two different types of attack: you are targeting the pest with one product and the pest with another, and the second product acts at a different point in its life cycle. A spray too strong for the pest does nothing but put more product on the plant, which is wasteful and can harm people and the environment. The correct action is to identify the problem exactly, to use the right product at the right rate, and to repeat the correct application. If you are unsure, ICAT can help you identify the pest and give you the correct product.

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

When the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, spray a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel, never using neem powder alone. One kilogram of this mixture is enough for about 1,500-2,000 plants, so calculate the required amount for your field. Repeat the spray every 8-10 days while the crop is still young. Do not use neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the plant. Finally, consult ICAT for any variety advice that suits your area.

Because it is Striga, you must pull the weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material to stop seed spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure and some urea and earth up to weaken the parasite. Finally, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. history.content: my sorghum looks yellow because of nutrient deficiency, right?

draws.answer: No, nutrient deficiency does not make sorghum look yellow; yellowing of the lower leaves is a sign of nitrogen shortage in a soil that has lost organic matter. To see if it is nitrogen depletion, pull a handful of leaves, keep them in a bag, and let them cure in the shade while you wait for the test. After that, return the crop residues to the soil by adding manure, using compost, or leaving the residues in the field instead of burning them. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide, because they will not solve the shortage. After these steps, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the appropriate fertilizer dose for your plot.

The yellowing of the lower leaves shows nitrogen shortage in a soil that has lost organic matter, not a disease. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide on the seller's word because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on such soils. Begin by adding organic matter like manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the soil rather than burning them. Then rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, visit ICAT for a soil analysis and the appropriate dose for your plot.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: You are dealing with leucaena poisoning, a common sign of a deficiency in leucaena. Reduce the amount of leucaena in the diet to roughly a quarter to a third and avoid letting it dominate the ration. Introduce the reduced leucaena gradually over several days. Always provide your goats with clean water and a source of mineral or salt. If appetite does not recover, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, contact the veterinary service.

This is leucaena poisoning, which is caused by mimosine building up when leucaena makes up too large a share of the diet. Cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never the main feed. Mix the reduced leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Introduce any feed change slowly over several days. Keep clean water always available and give a mineral or salt block. If the goats keep dying, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

draws.answer: Fever, swollen throat, and mouth or throat lesions with fever in your goats are signs of a tick-borne disease. Call the veterinary service today because only they can tell whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the proper drug and dose. Mention the urine colour to the vet; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. Do not use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will supply the correct medication and dosage.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of cassava bacterial blight. Immediately uproot and destroy every cassava plant that is infected. After you have cleaned your tools, disinfect them before you move to the next plant. Then select cuttings only from plants that have no yellow streaks and no brown corky rot. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for the following season. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact an ITRA representative or a registered producer.

Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the cassava plants that show strong yellow mottling and abnormal leaf deformation because no spray will cure them. For the next planting, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no mottling. Avoid any cuttings from plants with the yellow or twisted leaves. Plant a resistant cassava variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed attacking your sorghum. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3-5 seeds per pocket at 3-5 cm deep and using 6-8 kg per hectare of treated seed. Weed the field at 2-3 weeks after sowing and then repeat the weeding at about 10 days. When the plants reach tillering, apply 2-3 kg of Urea per hectare to keep the shoot growth in check. Late in the season, about 30-45 days after sowing, insert Striga-harvesting powder or a similar product as described by ICAT or ITRA. If you need a specific product or dosage confirmation, see ICAT.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches to sorghum (hypnozes) during flowering, and you must pull it out at the first signs of growth. First, check your sorghum plants for tiny purple or grey-flowered plants that climb the stems, which are the signs of Striga. Pull those plants out immediately as soon as you see them, not later. Then weed the field to keep the sorghum field clean. Finally, choose a cereal like maize or millet as the next crop to avoid Striga from re-attacking. If you need more help, go to ICAT to confirm the problem.
